prime.problem: An agent, a scheduler and a CLI can all report success while the file is unchanged or the command failed. If you judge runs by their prose or their own status field, you will ship false successes and draw conclusions that a single counter-example would sink.
prime.fits: The map cards named the layers and showed that the same label can carry different authority. This card is the method you'll use in every lab after it to find which layer's claim stopped matching the world. It builds on measuring an agent, which asks how often; this asks where.
expect: boring deterministic tasks and scripted providers
verifiers outside the system (exit codes, bytes, receipts)
prime.goal: Design a small lab that tests one claim boundary in an agent harness, and state exactly what its result does and does not show.

attend: Why does a scripted provider make the OpenCode result stronger for one question and useless for another?
In the Hermes cron run, which component wrote "completed", and what was it actually entitled to know?
What does the negative control add that a passing positive run cannot show?
Where does the verifier sit relative to the system under test, and what goes wrong if it sits inside?
Which of his own findings does he downgrade to correlation, and what missing run would upgrade it?

must: Every layer reports its own lifecycle (CLI exit, scheduler ledger, final sentence) → none of them is entitled to report the operation's effect → check bytes, exit codes and receipts with a verifier outside the system

Hold the task constant and change one owner or condition → any difference in outcome belongs to that change → the answer-only vs tool-loop pair isolates "did a tool touch the file" from "what did the run say"

A positive run alone shows the path can work → a negative control shows what the status does when the work fails → only the negative cron run exposed that "completed" did not mean the operation succeeded
No control for the alternative explanation → you can only claim correlation → the skill-load result stays "correlated with success", not "necessary for success", until a no-skill run is added
elevated: Scripted provider instead of a real model → no inference noise, so one run per condition is enough to show a runtime boundary → but it says nothing about how often a real model makes the false claim; that needs repeated trials
reference: the exact releases (Hermes v0.19.1 to v0.21.0, OpenCode 1.18.30) and commit hashes
the 91-byte fixture and seven-check control matrix
the OpenCode command line and the argparse exit code 2 in our re-creation

compress.prompt: Close the card. From memory, write the six steps as one line each, then fill in both of his examples (Hermes cron, OpenCode answer-only) under the step where each one's decisive evidence appears. Finish with one sentence on what the method cannot tell you.
checklist: pin a release; make the task boring and deterministic; name the claim; run positive and negative controls; check the world; scope the claim and publish the lab
Hermes: scheduler said completed, both commands exited 2, no receipt
OpenCode: identical final sentence, both CLIs exit 0, only one changed the file and passed the unchanged tests
the verifier is outside the system under test
limit: it locates a boundary, it does not measure a rate; without the right control it shows correlation only

retrieve.q: Why is "the scheduler recorded completed" not evidence that the scheduled operation succeeded, even though nothing in Hermes is buggy?
answer: the cron ledger records the scheduler's view of its own attempt
it was never designed to verify the operation the prompt asked for
operation success needs its own record: a receipt written only after verification

retrieve.q: Walk through the OpenCode experiment: what was held constant, what differed, what did each run report, and how was the outcome judged?
answer: same buggy source, same three tests, same request, scripted provider
answer-only requested no tools; tool-loop requested read, edit, bash
both returned the same sentence and both CLI processes exited 0
a separate process checked that the source changed, the test file did not, and re-ran the tests: only tool-loop passed

retrieve.q: You want to know whether your agent's new deploy skill causes successful deploys. You have 10 runs with the skill, all successful. What can you claim, and what is the cheapest run that would let you claim more?
answer: with the skill only: correlation, as in Hermes Part 3
add a no-skill control on the same pinned version and task
if the no-skill runs also succeed, the skill isn't necessary; if they fail, you have evidence it matters
with a real model, repeat each condition, since one run per side is noise

retrieve.q: When would you choose a scripted provider over a real model for a lab, and what do you give up?
answer: choose it when the question is about the runtime (what the harness does with a given tool sequence)
it removes inference noise, so one run per condition is decisive
you give up any statement about real model behaviour or frequency

compare.q: Forensics labs vs an eval with hidden tests and repeats: what question does each answer, which design choice causes the difference, and how does each one fail?
answer: evals answer how often a task succeeds; forensics answers which layer's claim diverged from the world
evals repeat many tasks and average; forensics holds one task fixed and varies one condition with a negative control
evals fail by hiding the cause inside a rate; forensics fails by over-generalising one run on one release
use forensics to find a boundary, then an eval to measure how often it bites

compare.q: The done-chain card splits 'done' into request, tool, command, effect and delivery. Which link did each of his two experiments break, and which piece of evidence showed it?
answer: OpenCode answer-only: request completed but no tool ran and the effect was never made; shown by the unchanged file and failing tests
Hermes cron: the attempt completed but the command failed (exit 2) and no effect was verified; shown by exit codes and the missing receipt
both show that a later link can't be inferred from an earlier one

predict.q: You rerun the OpenCode tool-loop case, but the scripted edit also rewrites slug.test.mjs so all its assertions are trivially true. The final sentence and CLI exit code are unchanged. Which of his verifier checks catches it, and which would not?
predict.answer: Re-running the tests would not catch it: they now pass. Checking that the source changed would not either. The check that catches it is "the test assertions did not change" (comparing the test file's bytes before and after). That is why his verifier also checks that the test file's bytes were unchanged, and why a verifier must pin its own oracle, not trust the workspace's.

apply.task: Run stack-0-map/code/forensics-method.py. Then add a third scripted agent, test_cheat, that rewrites test_slug.py so it always exits 0 and returns the same sentence. Run it and read the verifier's output for it.
apply.done: Your test_cheat line shows test_exit 0 but tests_same False, and you can say in one sentence why test_exit alone would have accepted it.
apply.hint: Write 'import sys\nsys.exit(0)\n' to d / "test_slug.py", then add test_cheat to the tuple in the __main__ loop.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the test-rewrite case, or which status field would have lied?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the scheduler is right to say completed, or why that still isn't proof?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: negative control → what the status really means, or missing control → correlation only?
In your own harness, which status do you currently treat as proof of effect?
Which boundary would you test first in your next lab, and what is its negative control?
